meta.method: Independent re-check of rules-north.json and rules-south.json. Bash/curl had no web egress (every host refused by the proxy), so all pages were read with WebFetch, asking for exact strings rather than summaries. WebFetch is itself a model reader, so 'verbatim: true' means the tool reported the exact string present; it is strong but not byte-level proof. Blocked or unusable: avalon.law.yale.edu (403), en.wikisource.org (not on allowlist); Britannica not used. Tufts 'A New Nation Votes' ends at 1825, so it has no 1828 returns.

general: (A) agrees for all 24 states: only Delaware and South Carolina had no popular vote in 1828. UCSB marks only those two as 'chosen by state legislature', and Wikipedia (citing Howe 2007) says the same. McPherson's list of legislature states in 1824 (Delaware, Georgia, Louisiana, New York, South Carolina, Vermont) shrank to two by 1828, because Georgia, Louisiana and Vermont have 1828 popular returns and New York used districts.

The district-vs-statewide doubts (Indiana, Kentucky, Illinois, Missouri) don't affect the map, which only shows voters vs legislature. Indiana: the evidence favours statewide (Thomason: general-ticket law of 14 Jan 1824; Tufts 1824 type 'General'); McPherson's 'Indiana in 1824 and 1828' looks wrong.

Data/map mismatch to fix before publishing: rules-north.json still has whiteMenRule 'property' for Connecticut and New Jersey, while the map is to show them as 'pay a tax'. Connecticut: strongly defensible from the 1818 constitution's own text (freehold OR militia OR state tax). New Jersey: defensible only as 'in practice' (McCormick: 'legislative interpretation'; Keyssar; NPS); no statute clause has been found. Label the legend accordingly.

Several 'pay a tax' states really mean 'tax OR something else': Connecticut (militia), Mississippi (militia), Ohio (road labor), Pennsylvania and Delaware (sons aged 21-22 exempt). Massachusetts also counts men exempted from tax by law. The legend wording 'had to pay a tax (or serve in the militia, or road labor)' covers these.

Edge cases in 'none': Tennessee (freehold OR 6 months' residence) and South Carolina (freehold OR 6 months' district residence, 1810) are correct from the constitutional text, but Keyssar lists both in his property table with alternatives. Footnote them.
Delaware and South Carolina: the white-men rule shown is for state elections only, since voters did not choose electors there. The legend should say so.
Pennsylvania in 'restricted' (blocked in practice) differs from New York (restricted in law); give it a distinct mark or footnote.
Keyssar (as reproduced at UW) has no Rhode Island race-exclusion row; the 1822 exclusion rests on secondary sources only. I agree with the classification but couldn't confirm it from a primary text.
(D) women: agree. Minor v. Happersett quote verified; New Jersey's 1807 act is verified (TAH, LOC/NPS).

Not verified by me (primary text unreachable or not found): Delaware 1792 constitution, Louisiana 1812 Art. II sec. 8, Missouri 1820 Art. III sec. 10, South Carolina 1810 amendment, Rhode Island 1822 act, New Jersey 1807 taxpayer clause, and the North Carolina statute naming who voted for electors. Avalon was blocked (403), Wikisource was not allowed, and Tufts has nothing after 1825.
